Tired of Struggling with Stubborn Jars?
Say goodbye to the frustration of opening jars with the Effortless Jar Opener! 🏆💪

With its ergonomic design and powerful grip, this handy tool makes opening even the toughest jars a breeze. Whether you have arthritis or just want to save time in the kitchen, the Effortless Jar Opener is here to help!
Here’s the quickest, easiest way to keep your food fresher for longer! 👀

Tired of Struggling with Stubborn Jars?
Say goodbye to the frustration of opening jars with the Effortless Jar Opener! 🏆💪

With its ergonomic design and powerful grip, this handy tool makes opening even the toughest jars a breeze. Whether you have arthritis or just want to save time in the kitchen, the Effortless Jar Opener is here to help!

My orthopedist told me to stop knitting.

The appointment lasted six minutes. He looked at the X-ray, not my hands. He said "basal thumb arthritis" and "avoid the aggravating activity."

I said, "The aggravating activity is knitting. And crochet. I've been doing both for forty-one years."

He said, "Then you'll need to find a different hobby."

He handed me a recovery pamphlet with a golfer on the cover. Nothing inside about knitting. Nothing about crochet. Nothing about the way my thumb works a stitch a thousand times an evening.

It was written for golfers and jar-openers. Not for knitters.

He never asked to see how I hold my needles. Not once.

I've never felt so dismissed in my life.

I'm sixty. Knitting has got me through the death of my sister, the end of my marriage, and forty Christmas seasons. It's more than making things. I'd be lost without it.

It's not a hobby I can swap out like a streaming subscription. And he spent six minutes on it.

I stopped for three weeks.

The pain calmed down.

Then I picked up my needles and lasted nine minutes. Three weeks of rest. Nine minutes before that click came back at the base of my thumb. Maybe worse than before.

My second doctor recommended cortisone. The cortisone was okay for a while. Then the click came back at minute twelve. The third doctor said, "Sometimes we have to accept that our bodies change."

Three doctors. Three versions of "stop." I wasn't being treated. I was being dismissed.

I'd also tried so many different types of brace — all not designed for knitters.

A rigid thumb splint that locked my whole thumb. Couldn't hold the needle. Made for someone who jammed their thumb, not for someone working a row of stitches.

Compression gloves that squeezed my fingers while the base of my thumb — the joint that was actually giving way — had nothing around it. Made for general arthritis. Not for knitting.

A soft neoprene wrap that felt nice but didn't stop the bones from sliding. I couldn't get on with it at all. Not one of them gave me support where I actually needed it.

Three braces. Not one of them made for knitting. Because knitting is not the same as gripping a golf club, or typing, or opening a jar.

The small, repeated movement your thumb makes working a stitch — knitting or crochet — is one that nothing else copies. And nobody was designing for it.

In March my friend Donna told me about a hand therapist who works with crafters. Donna knits and crochets, same as me. "She asked me to show her how I hold the hook," Donna said. "No doctor has ever done that."

The hand therapist's name was Claire. Before she looked at my X-ray, she asked me to pick up my needles and show her how I knit.

She watched the base of my thumb. She asked me to pinch her finger. The click was immediate. She felt the bones shift.

She said, "The joint is sliding."

She explained it simply. The base of the thumb is a saddle joint. After forty-one years of knitting and crochet, the ligaments holding it in place have gone loose. So every time you work a stitch, the joint slides. The bones shift past each other. That's the click. That's the collapse. That's the pain.

The joint is sliding. That's the whole problem.

Rest didn't hold because the ligaments are still loose — first stitch back, the joint slides again. Cortisone didn't last because it calms the swelling but doesn't stop the sliding. One session of knitting and it's back.

Then she said the part that changed everything.

"Even if those braces had sat in the right place — none of them were made for the way a knitter's thumb actually moves."

She said the movement of working a row is one that nothing else copies. A brace built for a golfer's grip is no use for the way a knitter's hand works a needle. The movement is different. The support has to be different — and it has to sit where the joint is giving, with support further up the thumb, not just hugging the wrist.

She gave me a stabiliser made specifically for knitting and crochet. Not for athletes. Not for jar-openers. For the way a crafter's thumb actually has to move.

It wraps the base of the thumb. Holds that one sliding joint steady. Doesn't lock anything. The thumb still works the needle. The other fingers stay free.

Rigid braces hold the joint but kill the movement. Soft wraps allow the movement but don't hold the joint.

This did both. Because it was made for the movement knitters and crocheters actually make.

Not locked. Held.

"If the joint stops sliding," she said, "the grinding stops. The collapse stops. That's it."

I went home. Put it on. Picked up my needles. Worked a row.

No click.

Twenty minutes in, I could feel the yarn.

I could set my tension.

Everything worked.

But the joint wasn't sliding.

Forty-five minutes in, I was knitting the way I used to before any of this started.

I knitted for an hour and a quarter that night. When I stopped, I was furious. Because three doctors had spent eighteen minutes combined and told me to stop.

One hand therapist spent forty-five minutes, watched my thumb actually move, and gave me something made for the way my hands actually work.

Not a golfer's hands. Not a jar-opener's hands. A knitter's hands. A crocheter's hands.

It's been seven weeks.

I knit and crochet every night. The collapse is gone. The click wasn't there. The joint isn't sliding, because something is finally holding it steady during the exact movement that was making it slide.

I cancelled my follow-up with the orthopedist. The one with the golfer pamphlet.

If a doctor told you to stop knitting or crocheting because of your thumb — the joint is probably sliding. Nothing made for golfers or jar-openers will hold it. The movement of working a row is not one those products were ever built for.

When the brace is made for the way a knitter's thumb moves — holding the joint steady while you work, without killing the movement — the sliding stops.

Three doctors told me it was over. A hand therapist and a brace made for my actual hands showed me it wasn't.

Use it or lose it. I'm not losing it.

Link is here: https://handhearth.com/products/knitting-thumb-wrist-stabiliser
